1. Introduction
Prevalence rates for cannabis use have steadily increased in recent years, with approximately 18.1 million individuals reporting marijuana use within the past month on a National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) conducted by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA, 2012). Over the past two decades, an extensive growing body of research has demonstrated that cannabis use adversely affects cognitive performance among measures that target attention (Abdullaez, Posner, Nunnally, & Dishion, 2010; Medina, Schweinsburg, Cohen-Zion, Nagel & Tapert, 2007; Solowij, Michie, & Fox, 1995; Solowij et al., 2002), working memory (Kanayama, Rogowska, Pope, Gruber, & Yurgelun-Todd, 2004), verbal learning and memory (Hanson et al., 2010; Harvey, Sellman, Porter, & Frampton, 2007; Lisdahl & Price, 2012; Mathias et al., 2011; McHale & Hunt, 2008; Medina et al., 2007; Tapert, Granholm, Leedy, & Brown, 2002), and executive functions (Battisti et al., 2010; Gonzalez et al., 2012; Grant, Chamberlain, Schreiber, & Odlaug, 2012; Lisdahl & Price, 2012; Pope & Yurgelun-Todd, 1996; Ranganathan & D'Souza, 2006; Schuster, Crane, Mermelstein, & Gonzalez, 2012; Solowij et al., 2012).
Delta 9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive agent of the cannabis sativa plant, is thought to be responsible for the cognitive effects of smoked cannabis (Bisogno, & Di Marzo, 2010; Grotenhermen, 2003). Briefly, THC acts by binding to CB1 receptors that are largely distributed through the central nervous system and aids in several important functional roles that modulate neural responses (Gerdeman, Ronesi, & Lovinger, 2002; Heifets & Castillo, 2009; Yasuda, Huang, Tsumoto, 2008).
1.1. Effects of cannabis on cognition
Comprehensive reviews of the cannabis and cognition literature are available (see Gonzalez, 2007; Grant, Gonzalez, Carey, Natarajan, & Wolfons, 2003; Hart, van Gorp, Haney, Foltin, & Fischman, 2001; Lisdahl, Thayer, Squeglia, McQueeny, & Tapert, 2013; Schreiner & Dunn, 2012), which generally support the adverse acute effects of cannabis on cognition; however, non-acute effects remain less clear. Grant et al. (2003) reported that average effect sizes across studies of learning and forgetting among cannabis users were rather small in magnitude. In the same review, similar results were found across all domains of neurocognitive performance, suggestive of minimal adverse effects of cannabis use on neurocognitive performance. In amore recent meta-analysis, Schreiner and Dunn (2012) found that after at least 25 days of cannabis abstinence, there were no residual effects on cognitive performance. Gonzalez (2007) highlighted some of the methodological limitations across studies examining the non-acute effects of cannabis that include heterogeneous participant samples that differ in factors such as severity of substance use, length of abstinence, and the presence of comorbid substance abuse and psychiatric disorders. More recent studies highlighted the moderating role of genetic polymorphisms such as the COMT val158met and 5-HTTLPR genes on the relationship between cannabis use and cognitive performance (Verdejo-García et al., 2013).
Researchers (i.e., Pope, Gruber, Hudson, Huestis, & Yurgelun-Todd, 2001, 2002) have tested attention among current heavy cannabis users, former heavy cannabis users, and control subjects on days 0, 1, 7, and 28 of abstinence. On all four occasions, no significant between-group differences were found in attention performance despite impairments in other cognitive domains (i.e., learning and memory), which persisted up to 7 days of abstinence. After 28 days of abstinence, learning and memory impairments were no longer found. In a study that used a shorter abstinence period (i.e., 24 h), cannabis users showed both longer reaction times and delayed processing speed compared with controls (Solowij et al., 1995, 2002). Using fMRI, Chang, Yakupov, Cloak, and Ernst (2006) found that marijuana users and controls demonstrated similar task performance on visual attention. However, both active and abstinent marijuana users showed activation differences across prefrontal, medial parietal, and occipital brain regions during the task, suggesting neural adaptation in chronic marijuana users.
A recent longitudinal study (Meier et al., 2012) that examined the effects of cannabis use on IQ and neuropsychological functioning suggested that the long-term effects of cannabis use may be more profound, as demonstrated by a drop from childhood average to adult low-average full-scale IQ among cannabis users.
Frequency and amount of cannabis use have also been associated with neurocognitive performance in some studies. Studies have found that THC levels in urine are associated with the severity of cognitive impairment (Fried, Watkinson, James, & Gray, 2002; Pope et al., 2001). Using event-related potentials as a measure of brain functioning, Theunissen et al. (2012) found that THC significantly reduced P100 levels among heavy cannabis users. Similarly, Lane, Cherek, Tcheremissine, Lieving, and Pietras (2005) found that subjects exposed to a high dose of THC (3.6%) demonstrated significantly greater risk-taking than subjects receiving lower doses of THC.
Together, these studies suggest that the magnitude of adverse effects of cannabis on cognition varies depending upon the frequency of use, and length of abstinence. However, findings have been mixed, calling attention to the need to further systematically examine how level and frequency of cannabis may affect neurocognition among diverse and representative samples.
1.2. Comorbid alcohol use
Considering that 51.8% of the population reports being current alcohol drinkers and 31.3% of heavy alcohol users also report using illicit drug (SAMHSA, 2012), it is difficult to ascertain whether the observed neuropsychological deficits among cannabis users are the direct results of cannabis use. Recent evidence suggests that heavy drinking during adolescence and young adulthood is associated with poorer neurocognitive functioning during the young adult years (Brown, Tapert, Granholm, & Delis, 2000; Giancola, Shoal, & Mezzich, 2001; Hanson, Medina, Padula, Tapert, & Brown, 2011; Sher, Martin, Wood, & Rutledge, 1997; Tapert & Brown, 1999). Therefore, consideration of comorbid alcohol may be an important area of examination in studies of the effects of cannabis on neurocognition.
1.3. Hypotheses
The purpose of the current study was to examine the effects of cannabis use in a non-clinical sample of adults. We recruited individuals who reported recent cannabis use (in the last 4 weeks), remote cannabis use (longer than 4 weeks), and no use. We chose 4 weeks as our abstinence cut-point based upon the work of Pope et al. (2001, 2002). Our study hypotheses were as follows: (H1) recent users (i.e., those who reported using cannabis in the last 4 weeks) will demonstrate poorer neurocognitive performance than non-users and past users; (H2) past users will demonstrate poorer performance than non-users, although to a lesser degree than recent users; (H3) among recent and past cannabis users, abstinence (of cannabis) will be associated with higher neurocognitive performance; and (H4) among recent users, frequency of cannabis use in the last 4 weeks and number of times used per day will be negatively associated with neurocognitive performance. Alcohol use variables (frequency and amount used) were included in statistical models as covariates to control for the effects of alcohol when examining the effects of cannabis on neurocognitive performance.
2. Method
2.1. Participants
Participants were recruited through fliers distributed around local college campuses and the community as part of a larger study examining psychosocial factors involved in neurocognitive test performance among African Americans and Caucasians. All participants were screened for neurological, psychiatric, and medical confounds using the Structured Clinical Interview (SCID) for DSM-IV (First, Spitzer, Gibbon, & Williams, 1995), Mini-mental Status Exam (Folstein, Folstein, & McHugh, 1975), and questionnaires about neurological and medical history. Institutional Review Board approval was obtained prior to beginning study procedures. All participants provided written informed consent. Approximately 176 participants completed the study; however, 18 participants were excluded because they also reported use of stimulants or hallucinogens. One hundred and fifty-eight participants remained for testing study hypotheses. Participants were grouped as follows based on their reported cannabis use: recent users (n = 68), past users (i.e., more than 28 days; n = 41), and non-users (n = 49). Please see Table 1 for participant demographics.
2.2. Measures
2.2.1. Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Disorders (SCID)
Past and present substance abuse and psychiatric status was determined using the SCID for DSM-IV (First et al., 1995). The SCID is a semi-structured interview for making DSM-IV Axis I diagnoses.
2.2.2. Brief Drug Use History Form
The Brief Drug Use History Form(DHQ) is a questionnaire created by the University of California, Los Angeles' Center for Advanced Longitudinal Drug Abuse Research to facilitate cross-project analysis. It collects information on inhalants, marijuana/hashish, hallucinogens, amphetamines, barbiturates, opiates, cocaine (crack/freebase and powder separately), tranquilizers, PCP, ecstasy, synthetic drugs, alcohol, and tobacco. Participants underwent urine toxicology screening, using Integrated E-Z Split Key (Innovacon, Inc., San Diego, CA), a test that utilizes monoclonal antibodies to selectively detect elevated levels of specific drugs in urine. The following drugs were tested: amphetamine, methamphetamine, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, buprenorphine, cocaine, marijuana (THC), MDMA, opiates, oxycodone, phencyclidine, propoxyphene, and nortriptyline.
2.2.3. Neurocognitive assessment
Participants were administered a brief cognitive test battery that included measures with demonstrated validity, including tests of premorbid intellectual ability (Wechsler Test of Adult Reading [WTAR]; Wechsler, 2001), attention/working memory (Trail Making Test — Part A; Reitan, 1958; Stroop Test [Color and Word conditions]; Golden, 1978; Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale — IV [WAIS-IV; Wechsler, 2008] Letter-Number Sequencing subtest), speed of information processing (WAIS-IV Digit Symbol and Symbol Search subtests), learning and memory (Brief Visual Memory Test-Revised [BVMT-R]; Benedict, 1997; Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised [HVLT-R] Immediate and Delayed subtests; Brandt & Benedict, 2001), and executive functioning (Trail Making Test — Part B; Reitan, 1958; Stroop Test (Color–Word condition)). All raw scores were converted to standardized t scores using published normative procedures (Heaton et al., 1995) and grouped by cognitive domain. Global neuropsychological performance was calculated by averaging t scores from individual cognitive tests, which is considered a standard approach to interpreting neurocognitive data (Heaton et al., 1991; Miller & Rohling, 2001). Cronbach's alpha of the global neurocognitive performance scale was .92.
3. Statistical analyses
3.1. Tests of assumptions
Distributions for all measures were inspected for normality and linearity. Several of the drug frequency variables violated assumptions of normality. Logarithmic 10 transformations were applied to skewed variables, which resulted in normal distributions. Transformed variables were then used in Pearson correlational analyses with neurocognitive performance. Global neurocognitive performance and premorbid IQ were normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk'sW= .97, df = 157, p = .34 & Shapiro–Wilk'sW=.91, df = 157, p =.32 respectively).
Analysis of variance and chi-square analysis were used to examine demographic differences between cannabis groups that are associated with neurocognitive performance. Correlational analyses between those demographic variables that differed between cannabis groups and neurocognitive test scores were conducted to determine whether they should be included in the models.
3.1.1. Group comparisons
Groups significantly differed in age, F(2, 155) = 22.1, p < .001, η2 = .22. Post hoc tests revealed that past users were significantly older than recent users and non-users. Age was negatively associated with performance on measures of attention/working memory, r(156) = −.17, p = .03. Groups did not significantly differ on education, F(2, 155)= 2.56, p = .08, η2 = .03 or ethnicity, χ2 (2, n=158)= 14.76, p=.14, η=.06. However, groups significantly differed in gender composition, χ2 (2, n = 158) = 19.39, p < .001, η = .35. Specifically, males were more likely to report recent use of cannabis than females (57% vs. 24%, respectively). However, gender groups did not differ in neurocognitive performance, F(2, 155) = 0.94, p = .50, η2 = .02 and was not included as a covariate in subsequent analyses. Groups also demonstrated significant differences in premorbid IQ scores (as measured by the WTAR), F(2, 155) = 5.78, p = .01, η2 = .12 with past users and recent users demonstrating higher premorbid IQ than nonusers. WTAR was significantly correlated with global neuropsychological performance, r (157) = .47, p < .001. Cannabis users (recent and past) reported significantly more alcohol use than non-users. No other drugs (e.g., opiates, hallucinogens, and stimulants)were reported or detected in urine (based upon toxicology testing).
Please see Table 1 for percentage of individuals who reported alcohol use, abuse, and dependence among cannabis use groups.
3.1.2. Statistical procedures
To test H1 and H2, analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) controlling for age, premorbid IQ (i.e., WTAR), and frequency and amount of current alcohol use was conducted using cannabis group (i.e., recent users, past users, and non-users) as the independent variable and global neurocognitive t score as the dependent variable. Follow-up analyses were conducted with individual cognitive domain scores. Finally, a series of post-hoc tests were conducted to isolate group differences following statistically significant omnibus F-tests. To test H3, time since last use was correlated with global neurocognitive performance and individual cognitive domains. In testing H4, cannabis drug use frequency variables were correlated with global neurocognitive performance and individual cognitive domain scores. Given the number of statistical comparisons, we adjusted our alpha level using false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg, 2000) to control for Type I error. Power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 to determine the level of power based upon sample size, number of groups, and number of statistical covariates. With an alpha level of .05, we had 80% power for detecting medium effect sizes when performing ANCOVA.
4. Results
4.1. Hypotheses 1 & 2 (performed among all cannabis use groups)
ANCOVA revealed significant group difference in global neurocognitive performance, F(5, 152) = 3.855, p = .02, η2 = .09, among the cannabis use groups. Tukey's HSD post hoc tests revealed that recent users demonstrated poorer performance than past users and non-users. There were significant group differences in attention/working memory performance, F(5, 152) = 5.29, p < .01, η2 = .13, with recent users performing more poorly than past users and non-users. There were significant group differences in speed of information processing, F(5, 152) = 3.08, p = .05, η2 = .06, such that non-users performed better than recent users and past users. Recent users and past users demonstrated significantly poorer performance in executive functioning than non-users, F(5,152) = 6.09, p < .01, η2 = .15. See Table 1 for means and standard deviations on neurocognitive domains.
4.2. Hypothesis 3 (performed among recent and past users)
This hypothesis was not confirmed. Specifically, we did not find significant correlations between time since last use and global neurocognitive function, r(107) = .05, p = .64, or individual cognitive domains (all ps >.05).
4.3. Hypothesis 4 (performed among recent users)
Amount of times cannabis was used in the last 4 weeks was negatively associated with global neurocognitive performance, r(66) = −.52, p < .001, and cognitive domains of attention/working memory, r(66) = −.50, p < .001, learning/memory, r(66) = −.42, p < .001, information processing speed, r(66) = −.42, p < .001, and executive functioning, r(66) = −.48, p = .004. Similarly, amount of times cannabis was used per day was negatively associated with global neurocognitive performance, r(66) = −.52, p = .01, and cognitive domains of attention/working memory, r(66) = −.46, p < .02, learning/memory, r(66) = −.45, p = .02, information processing speed, r(66) = −.50, p = .001, and executive functioning, r(66) = −.47, p < .01.
5. Discussion
The purpose of the current study was to examine the relationship of cannabis use on neurocognitive performance among a non-clinical adult sample. A major strength of the current study was its comparison of the neurocognitive functioning of recent and past users while controlling for age, alcohol use, and premorbid IQ to better understand the effects of cannabis on neurocognition. Within our sample of cannabis users, we were interested in how abstinence and frequency of use contributed to cognitive performance. As expected, we found that recent users demonstrated worse neurocognitive functioning than past users and non-users in global neurocognitive performance and the domains of attention/ working memory, information processing speed, and executive functioning. However, past users only differed from non-users in the domain of executive functioning. These findings are generally consistent with findings from Pope and colleagues (2001, 2002) and further support the contention that 28 days is a sufficient period during which cognitive functions seem to recover. This could be due to the reversible downregulation of CB1 receptors that have been found to occur in a variety of cortical regions (see Hirvonen et al., 2012). However, our sample of past users did not perform at the level of non-users across most domains, suggesting that cannabis use may ultimately interfere with optimal neurocognitive performance. Executive functioning represents a broad range of skills and abilities, such as planning, self-monitoring, inhibiting prepotent responses, and altering behavior in response to changing task demands. Neuroanatomical evidence suggests that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and posterior association areas mediate a majority of these functions (Gunning-Dixon & Raz, 2003). Given that CB1 receptors are densely located in the prefrontal cortex, cingulate gyrus, and basal ganglia (Eggan & Lewis, 2006), deficits in executive functions may persist long after use. Our findings pertaining to executive dysfunction are consistent with other studies (Bolla, Elderth, Matochik, and Cadet, 2005; Crean, Crane, and Mason (2011); Ramaekers, Kauert, van Ruitenbeek, Theunissen, Schneider & Moeller (2006), suggesting that the long-term implications of impaired executive functions could result in problems with decision-making, impulsivity, and poor judgment.
Among our recent users, frequency of use was negatively associated with neurocognitive performance, demonstrating that severity of use is important when attempting to understand the neurocognitive effects of cannabis use among recent users. We were unable to precisely identify the independent and synergistic effects of alcohol since most of our cannabis use sample also reported recent alcohol use. title: Effects of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol in individuals with a familial vulnerability to alcoholism.
abstract: A family history (FH) of alcoholism accounts for approximately 50% of the risk of developing alcohol problems. Several lines of preclinical evidence suggest that brain cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) function may mediate the effects of alcohol and risk for developing alcoholism including the observations that reduced CB1R function decreases alcohol-related behaviors and enhanced CB1R function increases them. In this first human study, we probed CB1R function in individuals vulnerable to alcoholism with the exogenous cannabinoid Δ(9)-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ(9)-THC). Healthy volunteers (n = 30) participated in a three test day study during which they received 0.018 and 0.036 mg/kg of Δ(9)-THC, or placebo intravenously in a randomized, counterbalanced order under double-blind conditions. Primary outcome measures were subjective "high," perceptual alterations, and memory impairment. Secondary outcome measures consisted of stimulatory and depressant subjective effects, attention, spatial memory, executive function, Δ(9)-THC and 11-hydroxy-THC blood levels, and other subjective effects. FH was calculated using the Family Pattern Density method and was used as a continuous variable. Greater FH was correlated with greater "high" and perceptual alterations induced by Δ(9)-THC. This enhanced sensitivity with increasing FH was specific to Δ(9)-THC's rewarding effects and persisted even when FH was calculated using an alternate method. Enhanced sensitivity to the rewarding effects of Δ(9)-THC in high-FH volunteers suggests that alterations in CB1R function might contribute to alcohol misuse vulnerability.

Introduction
Women historically have a lower prevalence of cannabis use than men.1,2 Further, men tend to use a greater variety of cannabis products, including more prevalent use of high-potency cannabis products,2 and are at increased risk of certain cannabis-related harms such as driving under the influence of cannabis.1 Coupled with historical cultural associations between masculinity and being “high”,2,3 the higher prevalence of substance use among men has been used as justification to exclude women from substance use research.2–4
Yet, recent findings have highlighted a narrowing of the sex/gender gap in cannabis use prevalence.1 For example, the ratio of men-to-women using cannabis in the past month in the United States (US) declined from a high of 2.125 in 2002 to a low of 1.25 in 2020—which seems to be largely driven by an increase in women's cannabis use.5 Even more strikingly, youth data from Ontario show that, as of 2023, girls actually have a higher prevalence of cannabis use than boys.6 Furthermore, data from the US and Canada have suggested that cannabis legalization has led to a sharper increase in cannabis-related hospitalizations in women compared to men.1 For example, a cross-sectional study in Ontario found that the expansion of Canadian cannabis legalization in 2020 (including the legalization of edible products) was associated with a large increase in cannabis-related emergency department visits among women aged 18–44 years.7
Despite these shifts, male research participants are still over-represented in cannabis research. A recent review found that between 2000 and 2014, 77% of participants in published cannabis trials were identified as male.8 This clear sex/gender disparity in cannabis research is increasing in public health relevance as both use of cannabis and potential harms associated with use are increasing in women and girls.
One approach to better understand the health effects of cannabis is to examine the impact of sex on acute responses to cannabis using a human behavioural pharmacology paradigm. Sex is an umbrella term that refers to complex biological factors, including chromosomes, genes, hormones, and all their downstream effects. Sex-related biological processes have widespread physiological effects (e.g., modulation of the central nervous system) and can affect the way that drugs interact with bodies.9 Gonadal hormones like estrogens, progestogens, and androgens, which are differentially expressed across sexes, can influence drug-seeking behaviours in rodents and the experience of subjective drug states in humans.10–13 In animal models, female rodents show greater self-administration of cannabinoids than male rodents, yet this sex difference is reduced by ovariectomy (removal of the ovaries, and thus dramatic reduction in estrogen).14 Therefore, sex-related biological processes likely have a significant impact on acute responses to cannabis and long-term health effects of cannabis use.
However, it is important that we do not conflate sex with gender, another umbrella term that refers to socially constructed meaning about sexed bodies and includes dimensions such as identity and norms. Although sex alone (in the absence of gender) can influence some biological outcomes, such as prostate or ovarian cancers, the reality is that sex and gender are entangled in complex ways.15,16 Social determinants such as food security, housing, employment, and education all affect the distribution of health and wellbeing and are all gendered.15 These gendered social determinants affect individuals at complex biological levels, which is sometimes referred to as “embodiment” or “biological embedding”,15 and can directly influence brain health and function.17 Transdiagnostic risk factors for mental health and substance use disorders such as childhood maltreatment, stressful life events, and experiences of racial and other minority stressors are all subject to sex- and gender-related variability in both prevalence and in direct impacts on the brain.17 Furthermore, some humans have a configuration of sex and gender that does not fit into the simplified binary systems historically employed in the biomedical sciences. Transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people have a gender identity and/or expression that does not align with the sex they were assigned at birth, while intersex people have a complement of sex characteristics that do not fit into historical definitions of “female” or “male”. TGD people are very rarely included in cannabis use research, despite TGD adults having significantly higher prevalence of cannabis use than cisgender adults,18 and virtually nothing is known about cannabis use in intersex people. We will explore these issues as caveats of this research approach throughout this article.
In a recent systematic review,19 we examined evidence from peer-reviewed articles for sex differences in the acute effects of cannabis on cognitive performance in humans. We identified 29 articles that met our inclusion criteria, just six of which found any evidence that female and male participants show different cognitive performance changes after acute exposure to cannabis. While this could be interpreted as evidence that sex has minimal influence on the acute cognitive effects of cannabis, our results could be alternatively interpreted to reflect the growing need for hypothesis-driven sex-based approaches in experimental substance use research.
The goal of this Commentary is to outline current issues in sex- and gender-informed human behavioural pharmacology of cannabis, using our systematic review as an example of the scope of existing evidence, and to advocate for future research priorities to better characterize the role of sex (and potentially gender) in modulating acute responses to psychoactive drugs. We note that while our systematic review focused on cognitive outcomes specifically, this article will focus more broadly on acute responses to cannabis. Furthermore, our focus is primarily on sex differences research as this is the most common approach employed in human laboratory studies of cannabis effects, but we emphasize that sex differences research is just one example of a broader array of sex- and gender-informed research approaches.
Prior review
A full description of our methods for the systematic review can be found in our previous publication.19 Our review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines 20 and was pre-registered with PROSPERO (registration ID CRD42024547066). We included studies of adults aged 18 years or older who were considered to be healthy volunteers (i.e., not sampled from a patient population). Articles had to assess sex differences in the acute effects of cannabis/THC on cognition (i.e., in the hours after administration).
We conducted full-text screening of 169 articles and 29 were included in the final synthesis.21 –49 Six out of the 29 included articles (20.7%) found at least some statistical evidence for sex differences in acute cognitive effects of cannabis/THC, with generally greater cognitive effects in female participants.26,31,34,39,45,48
Current issues
In writing our systematic review, we noted one overarching limitation was the lack of hypothesis-driven sex differences research in the cannabis field. This is likely due to the low number of studies that planned to examine sex differences; across the 29 articles included in our review, just two studies clearly identified a sex difference analysis as the primary aim of the study,21,22 while nine studies conducted a secondary sex differences analysis of one or more larger parent studies,23,24,28–30,35,36,47,49 and the remaining 21 studies did not specify an aim related to sex. Characteristics of included journal articles.
Note: M: number of male participants; F: number of female participants; Tot: total number of participants in sample.
Aim: Was a sex differences analysis the primary aim of the study (PRI), a secondary analysis of one or more parent studies (SEC), or not clearly articulated as an aim of the study at all (NO)?
Power: Was a sex comparison considered in an a priori sample size calculation?
Design: Was sex considered in the design of the study (e.g., drug exposure visits scheduled during one menstrual cycle phase only)?

Measure: Was a specific measure(ment) of sex or gender clearly articulated in the article?

We focus on four specific issues: (1) the lack of studies powered to examine sex differences, which precludes making any firm conclusions about study results given dramatic variability both within and between sex categories; (2) the lack of clarity of sex and gender language; (3) the lack of consideration of within-sex variability; and (4) the lack of attention to social and behavioural variables that co-vary with sex.
Lack of a priori consideration of statistical power
Statistical power is a complex topic in sex differences research, as many researchers are reluctant to incorporate sex into their experimental design due to misconceptions about insufficient power.50 To address this misconception, Phillips and colleagues 51 ran simulations on artificial datasets to examine the results of different scenarios where a treatment effect is examined in two sexes. In brief, they found that in some scenarios (i.e., where there is a baseline sex difference or when treatment effects are similar across sexes), incorporating sex into a factorial analysis does not decrease power to detect a treatment effect.51 While they did find that power to detect a main treatment effect significantly decreased when there was a large sex by treatment interaction (e.g., opposing effects in each sex), there was still high power to detect the sex by treatment interaction itself.51 However, it is important to note that power calculations for interaction terms are complex and depend on numerous factors, including effect sizes of the simple slopes, the study design (e.g., parallel groups or crossover), and the shape of the interaction (e.g., a reversed interaction where the treatment effect is opposite in both subgroups, or a fully attenuated interaction where the treatment effect is zero in one group and large in the other).52 Thus, power considerations are imperative to consider in sex differences research where the goal is to examine an interaction term (e.g., a sex by treatment interaction), especially where we expect the interaction term is non-trivial.
Out of 29 articles included in our systematic review, none included an a priori power calculation that considered a sex comparison. Overall sample sizes (including male and female participants) ranged from n = 9 33 to n = 438,39 while male-to-female ratios ranged from 0.70 21 to 8.32 Across 32 samples (some articles included multiple study samples), 23 had more male than female participants, four had exactly equal numbers of male and female participants, and five had more female than male participants. Thus, more than 70% of study samples had more males than females, and just four of 32 samples (12.5%) had an equal number of male and female participants. This is noteworthy as power to detect an interaction decreases as sample sizes across subgroups become more unequal.52 Furthermore, there were seven samples with fewer than 10 participants in either the male or female groups. With small samples sizes, only a large magnitude effect would yield a significant result, which is unlikely to be the case.
In summary, power issues are complex in sex differences research, and yet have not been adequately considered in human laboratory studies of acute cannabis effects. Issues such as small sample sizes, unequal numbers in each sex group, and insufficient power to detect a significant sex by treatment condition interaction all likely obfuscate potential sex effects in cannabis research.
Lack of clarity in sex and gender language
To conduct rigorous sex and gender research, it is essential to ensure clear recording, measurement, and reporting of sex and/or gender, which requires that authors provide a definition of the sex or gender variable used in their analysis and a description of how that variable was measured.53 In the simplest scenario, this would mean using a demographics questionnaire that includes the question, “Were you assigned female, male, or intersex at birth”? Unfortunately, this important step in sex and gender research is often skipped, which is likely due to the historical conflation of sex and gender terms and lack of understanding of appropriate sex and gender terminology. Indeed, just two studies included in our review 21,24 defined sex (as sex assigned at birth). Despite the definition offered, one article 21 proceeded to refer to female participants as women and male participants as men, a practice that both conflates sex and gender and also risks misclassifying individuals who are transgender or gender-diverse. Furthermore, these same two studies 21,24 were the only studies to explicitly state how sex or gender were measured (both mentioned self-report of sex assigned at birth). Without clarity about how sex and/or gender were defined, measured, or recorded, we do not know with certainty that participants were appropriately classified according to their sexed characteristics or gender identity.
In summary, researchers should ensure that they provide a clear definition of sex and/or gender, describe how these variables were measured, and ensure that each participant is allocated to a sex or gender group that accurately reflects their physiological and lived experience. Unfortunately, these steps are not reflected in current human laboratory studies of acute cannabis effects.
Lack of consideration of within-sex variability
Although sex differences research is a useful approach for examining high-level subgroup differences (i.e., comparing “females” to “males”), it is erroneous to assume that “sex” itself is causally affecting study endpoints; rather, it is one or more sex-related variables (e.g., gonadal hormone levels, downstream sex chromosome effects) or other variables that co-vary with sex (e.g., gendered variables) that drive differences. For example, ovarian hormones such as estradiol and progesterone fluctuate across hormonal cycles (e.g., the estrous cycle in rodents, the menstrual cycle in humans) and this can cause significant variability in outcomes such as mood and substance use.11,12,54 Research in animal models has demonstrated how this can lead to “masked” sex differences, where female and male rodents do not differ when directly compared but females show significant differences at high- versus low-estradiol phases of the hormonal cycle.54 It is feasible that this is true in human studies as well, where lack of consideration of menstrual cycle stage can mask potential sex differences in responses to cannabis. Of the 29 studies included in our review, just two considered menstrual cycle phase and/or use of hormonal contraceptives. While two studies is too few to establish a pattern, it is still worth noting that both studies found significant sex differences. Aghaei and colleagues 21 included female participants taking hormonal contraception or scheduled THC exposure visits in the early follicular phase of the menstrual cycle. Doss and colleagues 26 excluded female participants taking hormonal contraceptives and scheduled THC exposure visits when menstruating participants were in the follicular phase of the cycle. Thus, reducing within-sex variability (e.g., variability related to the menstrual cycle) may increase the likelihood of detecting binary sex differences, if they do exist.
Further consideration of other sex-related factors (e.g., diurnal fluctuations in androgen levels or life-course fluctuations in gonadal hormones, such as menopause or previous pregnancy) may be necessary to clarify sex differences in acute responses to cannabis. Importantly, all gonadal hormones show significant life course changes (e.g., the significant drop in estrogens at menopause), which underscores the need to take a lifespan approach in sex differences research.50 All 29 of the articles included in our review included participant samples with mean ages in the 20s. Thus, we currently do not have any evidence to assess how sex differences in acute responses to cannabis might differ at different life stages, such as menopause or andropause.
In summary, we know that sex-related variables such as gonadal hormone levels show regular fluctuations, both in the short term (e.g., across the human menstrual cycle) and the long term (e.g., with ageing), yet these considerations are not currently considered in human laboratory studies of acute cannabis effects.
Lack of sex-disaggregated baseline and demographic data
When conducting a sex difference analysis, it is essential to ensure that sex groups are similar in terms of key demographic variables (e.g., age, race/ethnicity) and cannabis-related variables (e.g., past cannabis exposure, current cannabis use frequency, presence or absence of CUD symptoms). This is particularly important since we know that there are significant sex and gender differences in frequency of cannabis use, types of products used, age of initiation of cannabis use, and experience of CUD symptoms.1,9 Of the 29 articles included in our review, 11 articles included at least one sex comparison of baseline characteristics. This means that 18 articles (62%) did not show any sex-disaggregated data or examine differences in baseline characteristics that could explain potential sex differences in outcomes (e.g., female and male participants might have very different past exposures to cannabis, which could mask sex differences in acute outcome data).
In summary, we know that there are numerous variables that co-vary with sex (i.e., systematically differ between people of different sex categories), yet are not consistently or thoroughly considered in human laboratory studies of acute cannabis effects.
Summary of current issues
Taken together, these methodological limitations add the following complexity to interpretation of the existing evidence for sex differences in the acute effects of cannabis. First, we do not know whether groups of female and male participants were of sufficient number to detect a statistically significant group difference, if one does exist. Second, limitations with measurement and reporting of sex and gender variables mean that we are not confident that all participants fell into a group that best matches their physiology and lived experience. Third, we know that there is meaningful variability within sex categories (e.g., hormonal fluctuations) that is not accounted for in the study design. Finally, we do not know whether the groups of female and male participants had similar social identities and lived experiences, which could meaningfully influence the way that they respond to cannabis. Thus, we argue that, at present, we do not have sufficient evidence to conclude whether sex has a meaningful impact on the acute effects of cannabis.
Future research directions
To move forward, we will need laboratory studies of the acute effects of cannabis that consider sex in their factorial analysis (whether powered or not to do so), as this evidence continues to shine light on potential sex differences to be explored in future studies. However, this approach is not sufficient; it will take intentional, hypothesis-driven sex differences studies (and ultimately, studies that move beyond sex differences) to clarify the relationship between sex and acute responses to cannabis.
